1230-pierre-grassou:
Honoré de Balzac tells of Pierre Grassou, a mediocre painter who, by copying the masters and flattering rich patrons, climbs into the bourgeois art world of Paris. His dull portraits sell, his betters starve, and a marriage plot tests whether money can buy him a place.

Balzac writes the art market with amused scorn: dealers, critics, and snobs all take their cut. Grassou himself is decent but dim, a man who succeeds by pleasing. The tale is a sharp little satire on taste and trade, and it shows Balzac's Paris in miniature.
12409-the-story-of-the-philippines-natur:
Murat Halstead, war correspondent and historian of the Philippine expedition, tells the story of the Philippines and America's new possessions after the war with Spain. The volume covers natural riches, industries, commerce, population, laws, habits, customs and scenery, with episodes of early history and the war itself.

Sketches and interviews feature Admiral Dewey, General Merritt, General Aguinaldo and the Archbishop of Manila, while Cuba, Porto Rico, Hawaii and the Ladrones enter the account. Halstead writes in a popular, illustrated style, mixing romance, tragedy and report. The book captures an American moment of empire, confident, curious and eager to describe its new Pacific world.
13357-cactus-culture-for-amateurs-being-:
W. Watson, assistant curator at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, writes a practical guide for amateur cactus growers in 1889. He describes the cactuses grown in Britain, genus by genus, from Epiphyllum and Cereus to Mammillaria, Opuntia, and Rhipsalis, with full notes on their botanic character.

Cultivation, propagation, temperature, and cleaning all get plain advice. Night flowers a foot long open in autumn, hairy stems are syringed with soft soap and warm water, and dealers are listed for buyers. Profusely illustrated, the book suits a Victorian parlour grower who wants rare plants to thrive far from Mexico and the desert sun.
14108-in-the-catskills-selections-from-t:
Houghton Mifflin gathered John Burroughs's Catskill writings in 1910, with photographs by Clifton Johnson. Contents run from snow-walkers and a white day with a red fox to phases of farm life, hemlocks, birds' nests, and the heart of the southern Catskills. Speckled trout and a bed of boughs close the set, with Slide Mountain, highest of the range, as frontispiece.

Birds give the book its music. A veery, smallest of the thrushes, salutes with whew notes and flute-like phrases, its breast spots dim beside the wood thrush's clear ovals. On Slide Mountain, Burroughs hears a new thrush song, finer and more under the breath than any other, and names it Bicknell's thrush. Fox hunters, hemlock shade, and farm seasons frame these encounters. Nature writing here stays close to eye and ear, and the Catskills emerge as a place to walk slowly and listen well.
16879-some-one-like-you:
James W. Foley wrote this 1916 book of verse, issued by P. F. Volland in New York, Chicago, and Toronto. The title poem praises a friend who makes the heart lighter, the day's work worthwhile, and a sigh half a smile. Life, it says, mixes briers and roses, clouds and sun, until the cloud lifts and shows some one like you, near and dear.

Foley writes short, song-like poems on friendship, loyalty, and cheer, in plain, warm lines. Each piece is brief enough to read aloud or to send to a friend. The book suits readers who like old gift-book verse: gentle, hopeful, and meant to comfort rather than to challenge.
18355-insights-and-heresies-pertaining-t:
Ammyeetis, signing as a Persian writer, published these fragmentary thoughts on the evolution of the soul in 1913, with a second edition in 1916 from the Christopher Publishing House of Boston. The dedication goes to heroic minds who can say my soul is my own and hold it against church or state. An opening anecdote borrows Emerson, whose farmer neighbor found his own ideas in Plato.

Contents move from no new thing and evolution to slowness of evolution and world making. They take up spirit individualized through matter and death as a benefactor. Later pieces treat the origin of evil, churches as money makers, heaven, nature spirits, and spiritualism. Readers get a short, independent spiritual philosophy: brief pieces that ask readers to test each thought against their own familiar thinking.
18625-contemporary-american-literature-b:
John Matthews Manly and Edith Rickert compiled this reference book at New York in 1922 with Harcourt, Brace and Company. It gives bibliographies and study outlines for contemporary American literature, opening with indexes to critical journals, general reference works, anthologies, and collections of plays, stories, and essays.

The core is an alphabetical index of authors with life notes, book lists, and studies and reviews, plus indexes by form, birthplace, and subject and local color. Students and librarians can trace a writer's work and its critics with ease. The book remains a useful guide to American writing of its era.
18894-then-i-ll-come-back-to-you:
Larry Evans published this novel in 1915, illustrated by Will Stevens, with Grosset and Dunlap in New York. Its frontispiece introduces a backwoodsman who has seen no more than three houses in a clearing before. He has never been out of the timber till today, and now aims to see more before he is done. That voice sets the book's tone.

The chapters follow the hero from a cheerful acceptance of a task through tangles of loyalty, faith, and love, toward the promised return of the title. Evans writes in a homely, humorous American voice. Readers get a light romantic adventure of rural America, with dialect, good nature, and a hero learning the wider world.
20053-the-rover-boys-in-the-air-or-from-:
Arthur M. Winfield published The Rover Boys in the Air in 1912, a boys' novel of flight. Its subtitle runs From College Campus to the Clouds. Dick Rover talks with Alexander Pop, the helper at the Rover homestead. Pop puzzles over the word biplane and what such a craft might be.

Early flight was still new and thrilling when the book appeared. The Rover Boys take that thrill from school grounds into the sky. Readers get period talk, jokes, and awe at a new machine age. The tale shows how boys' books raced to keep up with planes.
21430-mexico-and-its-religion-with-incid:
Robert A. Wilson travelled through Mexico in the early 1850s and wrote Mexico and Its Religion, published in 1855. He mixes scenes of travel with notices of past events tied to the places he saw. Santa Anna, the strongman of that age, stands at the front of the book.

Wilson argues hard points as he goes, including the roots of yellow fever. He charges the old Spanish historians of the conquest with lies, following Las Casas. His pages judge Mexican faith and rule from a firm Protestant, American view. Modern readers get both a travel record and a sharp sample of period opinion.
21949-hubert-s-wife-a-story-for-you:
Faith and marriage are tested in Hubert's Wife, a religious novel by Minnie Mary Lee published at Baltimore in 1873. Its motto warns that a way may seem right to a man, yet end in death. The contents promise a black conference, a missionary's retrospect, and a visitation by spirit and by death. Althea, the heroine guarded by others' choices, moves through christenings, prayer meetings, and a mysterious disappearance.

Hubert Lisle appears at Vine Cottage midway through the tale, and jealousy follows. The convert's trials and light after darkness close the long arc. Lee writes in the earnest evangelical manner of her decade, with deathbeds and awakenings. The novel is a period piece of American religious fiction, built to move the heart to decision.
22019-wisdom-wit-and-pathos-of-ouida-sel:
Ouida, born Maria Louise Ramé, was one of the most read English novelists of the Victorian age. In 1884 F. Sydney Morris gathered Wisdom, Wit, and Pathos of Ouida from across her books. The extracts come from more than twenty novels and tales. Among them are Chandos, Moths, Under Two Flags, and the much-loved A Dog of Flanders.

Morris chose passages for fine writing rather than plot. Roman fountains, soldiers, peasants, dogs, and proud beauties all speak in her rich, heated style. The selection shows why critics scolded Ouida and why the public adored her. It also serves as a handy first taste of a writer once found in every railway bookstall.
22261-a-ioyfull-medytacyon-to-all-englon:
Stephen Hawes, poet to Henry VII, wrote A Joyful Meditation to all England of the Coronation of Henry VIII. The poem greeted the young king's crowning in 1509. Hawes praises the famous clerks and poets who wrote nothing in vanity. They grounded their work on good morality, he says, and fumigated England's rude language with fair, sweet eloquence.

John Lydgate, the monk of Bury, stands as Hawes's model of the virtuous poet. The meditation urges the new king toward wisdom and just rule in allegory. Printed in the old black-letter spelling, the poem is hard going but historic. It shows Tudor court poetry welcoming a king whose reign would remake England.
2430-romantic-ballads-translated-from-th:
George Borrow translates Danish romantic ballads in this volume, bringing the songs of knights, mermaids, and elfin kings into English verse. The ballads tell of love, revenge, and the supernatural in the stark style of northern folk poetry, with Borrow's rugged translations matching their force. Miscellaneous pieces add his own poems and fragments.

Borrow, himself a wanderer and linguist, loved the literature of the road and the border. The collection preserves a tradition little known in English. Folklore and poetry readers will find a rare, vigorous book. Borrow learned Danish during his travels as a Bible agent in Europe.
24474-the-nursery-january-1873-vol-xiii-:
Published in Boston in January 1873 by John L. Shorey, this number of The Nursery, a monthly magazine for youngest readers, opens its thirteenth volume. Its prose pieces include the story of two English sparrows brought to America, a little teacher, Katy's Christmas presents, and a tale of horses jumping overboard.

Verse pieces include Christmas Morning, Santa Claus, and The Johnny-Cake, with The Lady-Bird set to music. Short, simple, and cheerfully illustrated, the magazine shows what American editors offered small children in the 1870s: gentle stories, holiday cheer, and lessons in kindness, told in words a beginner could follow.
25657-deborah-dent-and-her-donkey-and-ma:
Two humorous tales, priced at one shilling, fill this London picture book from Dean and Munday and A. K. Newman, embellished with seventeen beautifully coloured engravings. Deborah Dent and her donkey come first, with Madam Fig's gala second.

Deborah Dent had a donkey so fine, the verse begins, with marrowbones and cherrystones in a bundle jig. She kisses the sweet donkey, almost divine, with sparkling eyes, ambling and scambling, braying sweet, mane cropt and tail lopt, thistle fed and merry. A donkey turned schoolmaster fronts one tale, Johnny Fig and his wife another.
26368-the-ladies-book-of-useful-informat:
The Ladies' Book of Useful Information, compiled from many sources and printed at London, Ontario, in 1896, promises women a storehouse of facts in one volume. Its preface, addressed to the ladies of America, says every girl of twelve and up should read it, and every mother should place it in her daughters' hands. It claims to save money spent on cosmetics, medicines, and household goods.

The first chapter teaches personal beauty, youth, and health, with secrets the ancients knew and later ages found. Later pages turn to providence and adversity, noting that trouble may suit some souls better than prosperity, and that the poor are God's children no less than the rich. Marriage offers, or their absence, get calm, moral counsel. The book mixes household hints with Victorian advice.
28133-the-nursery-may-1877-vol-xxi-no-5-:
The Nursery for May 1877, volume twenty-one, number five, is another Boston monthly for youngest readers from John L. Shorey. Its lead tale, The Young Lamplighter, follows Wallace, a boy of ten, and his brother Charles as they light fifty lamps near Boston each night, Wallace riding a kind saddle-horse. Other prose covers a blind woman, an eider-duck, and a strolling bear.

Verse includes Popping Corn, the cooper's song, polliwogs, and Grasshopper Green, the last with music by Linda Cantoni. Drawing lessons and true stories of birds and pets fill the rest. The issue blends useful knowledge with gentle fun for small children.
28272-biographia-scoticana-scots-worthie:
Biographia Scoticana, or Scots Worthies, gives brief historical accounts of eminent Scots, chiefly reformers and martyrs, with notes on God's judgement and justice. The e-text, prepared from an old edition, keeps Scottish names and spelling, marks illegible words, and notes a page-number error after page 336. Greek is transliterated in braces.

Lives of ministers, soldiers, and sufferers fill the volume, told with Protestant earnestness. The book served generations of Scottish readers as a storehouse of godly example. Modern readers get a direct view of how Scotland once remembered its own heroes of faith.
3042-the-hispanic-nations-of-the-new-wor:
William Shepherd wrote The Hispanic Nations of the New World, a chronicle of southern neighbors, for the Chronicles of America series, published by Yale University Press in 1919. Chapters run from the heritage of Spain and Portugal through independence or death and ploughing the sea. The age of dictators, peril from abroad, greater and lesser states, the republics of South America, Mexico in revolution, the Caribbean, and Pan-Americanism follow. Shepherd follows figures such as Rosas, who rose in Buenos Aires in 1829 from stock farmer to ruler of the Argentine Confederation, becoming a despot of extraordinary character.

The book sets each nation's story against Spanish American capitals and neglected interiors. It gives North American readers a compact survey of Latin America on the eve of the nineteen twenties.
30581-notes-in-north-africa-being-a-guid:
W. G. Windham writes Notes in North Africa, a guide to the sportsman and tourist in Algeria and Tunisia. A new edition with coloured illustrations was published in London in 1862 by Ward and Lock. An illustration shows his two servants, Angelo and Nero, by R. Pheney.

A preface to the second edition answers two faults found with the first, starting with personal allusions that offended many people. Windham replies that offence was far from his mind, asks the offended to consider expressions unsaid, and omits them in this edition. The guide mixes travel advice, sport, and local observation for Victorian visitors to North Africa.
31766-five-hundred-mistakes-of-daily-occ:
Published in New York in 1856, this handbook lists five hundred common errors in speaking, pronouncing, and writing English, each set right. It was entered for copyright in 1855 by Walton Burgess. Its preface says the book is not a learned treatise, but a practical aid for people who misuse everyday words, twist grammar, and cloud their meaning.

Rather than teach grammar from first principles, it corrects mistakes one by one, so a reader can look up a fault and fix it at once. Readers get a mid-nineteenth-century usage guide, still readable as a record of what educated Americans then counted as correct speech.
32324-sam-this-is-you:
Murray Leinster's tale, printed in Galaxy in May 1955, follows Sam Yoder, a telephone lineman for the Batesville and Rappahannock Telephone Company. Sam, engaged to Rosie, has been working on a device to make private talk possible on a shared party line. Rosie admires his cleverness and believes a smart man like him should make something of himself, so Sam takes the project seriously.

The trouble starts about six in the evening on July second. Sam, up a pole near Bridge's Run hunting a dead party line, hears a voice cut in on his lineman's phone. The voice claims to be Sam himself. From there the story turns a small-town phone job into a puzzle about privacy, identity, and who is really speaking on the line.
34110-deadfalls-and-snares-a-book-of-ins:
A. R. Harding edited this book of instruction on deadfalls and snares, published at Saint Louis in 1907. Chapters cover building deadfalls. Bear and coon, otter and marten, and stone deadfalls follow, with the bear pen, portable traps, triggers, and trip triggers. How, when, and where to build, and the proper bait, follow.

Spring pole, trail set, and bait set snares, box, coop, and pit traps round out the book. A season's catch, skinning, stretching, handling, and grading follow, with the path from animal to market. Pictures show good deadfalls and their triggers. The book serves trappers who build their own traps.
36946-biography-of-rev-hosea-ballou:
Biography of the Reverend Hosea Ballou, by his youngest son Maturin Ballou, was published by Abel Tompkins in Boston in 1852. The book is dedicated to the Second Universalist Society of Boston, whose late pastor the elder Ballou had been.

The author's preface meets the obvious objection head on: a son, it may be said, cannot write a faithful history of a parent. Ballou pledges strict adherence to facts. Nothing will be suppressed, and not one iota added to the truth. No labored defence is offered, for no charges stand to refute. He had planned the work before his father's death. Minutes of dates and movements were kept over years. Short articles and memoranda from his father's own pen are embodied in the pages. The aim, he writes, is a simple, unvarnished biography.
37445-the-lady-and-her-horse-being-hints:
The Lady and Her Horse, compiled by Major Jenkins, was printed at Madras in 1857. Jenkins drew hints from various sources and shaped them into a system of equitation for women riders. A short address opens the book, quoting Colonel Greenwood on the chief point of horsemanship.

Greenwood holds that a rider must get the horse to be of her party, keen to obey and not just forced. The parts that follow treat dress, mounting, seat and balance, and the holding of the reins. Aids, guiding, and the paces of the horse come next, then leaping, road riding, and dismounting. Jenkins warns that many ladies think skill is just keeping the seat, and aims to give them full command.
387-vailima-letters-being-correspondence:
Robert Louis Stevenson writes to his friend Sidney Colvin from Vailima in Samoa in these letters, dated November 1890 to October 1894. The letters track his last years: building a house, planting, dealing with Samoan chiefs, and writing through ill health. Colvin, back in London, gets news, jokes, and drafts by slow mail.

Stevenson reports island politics, Samoan wars, and his own books in progress with candor and humor. The letters grow graver as his strength fails, yet they stay lively to the end. Together they form a vivid self-portrait of an author far from home, at work until his death.
41609-diary-of-john-manningham-of-the-mi:
John Manningham, a barrister of the Middle Temple, kept a diary in sixteen hundred and two and sixteen hundred and three. John Bruce edited the small book from the first copy, held in the British Museum. The Camden Society issued the edition in eighteen sixty-eight.

The first copy is a tiny volume, not quite six inches by four, with one hundred and thirty-three leaves. William Tite, head of the society, chose the diary for its varied interest. Manningham noted sermons, court talk, and London gossip of his day. Bruce added a preface essay on the man and his times. The diary gives a close view of Jacobean London.
41805-history-of-the-catholic-church-in-:
History of the Catholic Church in Paterson is a town faith past by Charles Shriner. A Press print house of Paterson brought it out in eighteen eighty three. Its full name adds a count of the fifty year feast of Saint John Church. Old folk with sharp minds gave most of its facts, the front word owns. Town writs were thin and poor, so their tales were checked with care.

Where doubt stood, Shriner gives his grounds for the form he takes as true. Part one treats first hurts on Manhattan Isle in the scheme. Faith men from New York, free land and free church, head that part. First faith men in New Jersey close the heads of that first part. Fast growth of the faith in Paterson is the theme of the whole.
43898-florence-nightingale-the-angel-of-:
Florence Nightingale, The Angel of the Crimea, A Story for Young People, by Laura Richards, was published by Appleton in 1909. Richards, author of Captain January, dedicates the book to a sister of Saint Mary who served the poor and sick for many years. She thanks Tooley's life of Nightingale and Kinglake's history for her facts.

Chapters follow Florence from her name and her three homes through the long wait for her call, then to the barrack hospital at Scutari. The lady with the lamp walks the wards in chapter eleven. A closing part takes up the tasks of peace. Generations of children met nursing's founder here.
44726-an-old-new-zealander-or-te-raupara:
T Lindsay Buick, author of Old Marlborough, wrote this life of Te Rauparaha, published in 1911 and dedicated to the Polynesian scholar Percy Smith. Its subtitle calls the Maori chief the Napoleon of the South.

The contents trace him from a warrior in the making through the land of promise and the southern raids to Wakefield and the Wairau. Later chapters make him the captive chief and weigh him in the balance. Illustrations show Kapiti, the memorial tiki on the site of the pa he destroyed at Kaiapoi, and a map of his raids. A lament on his capture, supposed sung by Te Rangihaeata, stands at the front. New Zealand readers get their great war-chief's biography.
45396-from-the-cape-to-cairo-the-first-t:
Ewart S Grogan and Arthur H Sharp wrote an account of the first traverse of Africa from south to north, dedicated to the memory of Cecil John Rhodes. Grogan calls Rhodes the greatest and most far seeing of British imperial statesmen. A letter from Government House, Buluwayo, dated September 7, 1900, opens the book. Its writer declines to compose an introduction, saying his correspondence runs by telegram.

He envies Grogan the journey instead. Grogan walked from Cape Town toward Cairo in 1898 to 1900, a feat of endurance through unmapped country. Nelson published the narrative. The traverse made Grogan famous at twenty five. Sharp shared the later stages of the march.
48373-from-paris-to-pekin-over-siberian-:
Victor Meignan's travel narrative From Paris to Pekin over Siberian Snows was edited from his French by William Conn and published in London in eighteen eighty-five. The subtitle maps the route in full. The traveller went by sledge over the snows of European Russia and Siberia. Then he crossed Mongolia by caravan, passed the Gobi Desert and the Great Wall, and rode by mule palanquin through China to Pekin.

Maps and many illustrations from the author's own sketches fill the book, with the Monastery of Troitsa as frontispiece. The preface to the English edition teases readers who are baffled by vague travel titles. A route this straight, the editor implies, deserves a title that says exactly what it is.
51838-personal-reminiscences-of-the-war-:
Personal Reminiscences of the War of 1861-5, by Morgan, was printed by Bell at Lynchburg, Virginia, in 1911. Its full title promises scenes in camp, on the march, on picket, on the skirmish line, on the battlefield, and in prison. Morgan dedicates the book to the memory of the loved ones at home: wife, father, and mother.

The contents march with his regiment from organization to Manassas. Blackburn's Ford and First Manassas come early, with the rebel yell and the gathering of spoils. The Peninsula campaign, Williamsburg, and Seven Pines follow, then Second Manassas, Sharpsburg, and Fredericksburg. Later chapters take in Gettysburg, the capture of Plymouth with its gunboat Albemarle, and the fighting around Petersburg.
51849-the-overland-route-to-the-road-of-:
The Overland Route to the Road of a Thousand Wonders is a railway travel book issued by the Union Pacific and Southern Pacific passenger departments in 1908. It pictures the journey from Omaha to San Francisco, eighteen hundred miles where bison and Indian once reigned. The line runs over the wagon trail of the pioneers. Its captions recall the days when an Indian arrow was shot for every spike driven.

The route crosses plains turned to farmland, climbs the Rockies, and skirts the Great Salt Lake. It crests the Sierra and drops through canyon and valley to the Golden Gate. The book sold the West to tourists by joining scenery to pioneer romance. It is a fine piece of railroad advertising from the age of steam.
51990-a-thrilling-narrative-of-the-minne:
A Thrilling Narrative of the Minnesota Massacre and the Sioux War of eighteen sixty two and sixty three was published at Chicago by A P Connolly in eighteen ninety six. Connolly was past commander of a Grand Army post. Graphic accounts treat the siege of Fort Ridgely and the battles of Birch Coolie, Wood Lake, and Big Mound. A portrait of Governor Alex Ramsey heads the book.

Thirty four years ago Minnesota was in an unusual state of excitement, the dedication opens. The great War of the Rebellion was on, and many of her sons were in the Union army, it says. Then the Sioux outbreak came, and troops hurried to the frontier, it adds. Company A of the Sixth Minnesota was sent to bury the victims and was itself surrounded at Birch Coolie, it notes. Veterans get a raw, illustrated war record.
5309-miss-lou:
E. P. Roe's Miss Lou, volume nine of his works, is dedicated to his youngest daughter, little Miss Lou. Its chapters open with a girl's protest, then follow something happening, Mad Whately, Aunt Jinkey's policy, Whately's idea of courtship. A storm begins, as dangers thicken and a whirlwind of events carries the story forward.

Later chapters bring a baffled diplomatist, Aunt Jinkey's warning, a threat, and Miss Lou emancipated, as the heroine finds her freedom. Roe writes a domestic Southern story of love, family, and independence, in the moral, popular style that made him a favourite of American readers.
55930-section-cutting-a-practical-guide-:
Sylvester Marsh wrote a small hand guide to cutting thin slices of tissue for study under the microscope, reprinted in New York in 1879 from the London form. Animal slices get the most space, as the full title says. Notes and an added part on the choice and care of section knives close the book.

Marsh wrote for the many new students who lacked time, funds, and big text books. Each step he gives was tried by his own hand, and he dwells on small points that trip up new workers. An added note for American readers clears up points that might puzzle them in the British text. The aim is sound daily craft, not new theory.
57407-my-merry-rockhurst-being-some-epis:
My Merry Rockhurst gathers episodes in the life of Viscount Rockhurst, a friend of King Charles the Second and once Constable of the Tower of London. Agnes and Egerton Castle recount the tales; Macmillan published the book in New York in 1907. A plate shows the plague year: through an open window comes the rumble of wheels, then the bell and the hoarse cry, bring out your dead.

The Castles wrote many historical romances together, among them The Pride of Jennico and Rose of the World. Egerton Castle alone wrote on fencing and the prince Othon. Rockhurst's episodes run through the court and the plague, in the voice of a cavalier looking back. The book belongs to the lush, costume school of its decade, fond of gallantry, duels, and dark London streets.
57589-silverspur-or-the-mountain-heroine:
Silverspur, or the Mountain Heroine, a tale of the Arapaho country, is number 212 of Beadle's Dime Novels, in the semi-monthly novels series. Beadle and Company of 98 William Street, New York, published the series that made the dime novel an American institution. The issue's own pages carry the machinery of the trade: the next number is advertised in full.

Number 213, to issue the following Tuesday, is Squatter Dick, or The Swamp Fox's Oath, by Jos E Badger Jr. Its advertisement recalls the old War of Independence in the Carolinas, where dwellings blazed and Marion became the Swamp Fox. Such back-page promotion kept readers buying number after number, and the series notice here boasts of the most widely circulated books of modern times. Silverspur itself is a western tale of the Arapaho country, sold for ten cents.
59675-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
The Index of the Project Gutenberg Works on Women's Suffrage maps a four-volume history. Widger compiled the index. The history itself was edited by Stanton, Anthony, and Gage. Steel engravings illustrated the original volumes. The years covered run from 1848 onward. This index prints each volume's contents in detail.

Chapter headings carry long descriptive sub-titles. They read like a narrative in miniature. The first volume opens with preceding causes. The world's anti-slavery convention of 1840 follows. Seneca Falls and the first woman's rights convention come next. State chapters proceed through Ohio and beyond. Sketches of early workers fill the summaries. Blackwell's letter and Rose's story are both noted. The index lets a reader find any episode across four volumes.
62165-from-dixie-to-canada-romances-and-:
H U Johnson wrote this history of the Underground Railroad, published in 1894, with his portrait as frontispiece. He dedicates it to the grandchildren of the generation that lived it, who must learn the story from lips and pages.

The preface explains the book's modesty: not a full history of slavery, but enough to make appreciable the cause of the Road. Secrecy, Johnson stresses, was its cardinal principle, and on the war's outbreak the subject was swallowed by greater excitements, leaving meager archives. In the eighties he researched systematically, gathering incident and information first published in the Home Magazine. Volume one offers romances and realities from a man who lived amid the excitements.
62845-pilgrim-guide-book-to-plymouth-mas:
The Official Pilgrim Guide Book to Plymouth, Massachusetts, by William Franklin Atwood, guides visitors to the shrines of the Pilgrim town. Copyright was taken in 1940, and this sixth edition appeared in May 1957 from the Memorial Press at Plymouth. It sold for twenty-five cents.

A guide map at the front shows the main streets and historic shrines. The book joins the tour to a brief outline of the Pilgrim migration and settlement. A motto from the gravestone of Governor William Bradford on Burial Hill urges readers not to relinquish what their fathers won with so much difficulty. A publisher's note points readers who want more to The Pilgrim Story, drawn from the writings of Bradford and Winslow. The colony seal, lost under Governor Andros and never found, is shown in facsimile.
63255-leon-burgos-and-salamanca-a-histor:
Albert F Calvert wrote Leon, Burgos and Salamanca, a historical and descriptive account in the Spanish Series he edited. John Lane, The Bodley Head, issued it in London and New York in MCMVIII. Four hundred sixty two illustrations fill the volume. Calvert dedicated it to the Marquis of Viana. Three long chapters carry the book, one for each city.

Leon opens at page one, Burgos at page thirty three, and Salamanca at page ninety six. The Leon plates begin with a general view and a view from the cemetery. Cathedral views follow in plate after plate. The door of the cross aisle, stained glass windows of two centuries, and the plan of the cathedral all appear. The lateral façade and the longitudinal section are drawn too. Art and travel readers get three Spanish cathedral cities in dense picture detail.
63388-the-development-of-british-landsca:
The Development of British Landscape Painting in Water-Colours, edited by Charles Holme with text by A J Finberg and E A Taylor, came out in 1918 as a Studio special number. The survey traces the English water-colour school from its early topographical work to the masters of the nineteenth century. Paul Sandby, the Cozens father and son, Thomas Girtin, and J M W Turner anchor the early chapters.

Later sections follow John Sell Cotman, David Cox, and Richard Parkes Bonington, and close with James McNeill Whistler and the painters of Scotland. Large plates carry the argument, letting readers watch the medium grow from tinted drawing into a full art of light and weather. The volume treats water-colour not as a lesser cousin of oil painting but as the field in which British landscape art did some of its most original work.
64979-youth-volume-1-number-5-july-1902-:
Youth, volume one, number five, is the July 1902 issue of an illustrated monthly journal for boys and girls. It was put out at Philadelphia by the Penn Publishing Company. Single copies cost ten cents, and a year cost one dollar. The frontispiece shows Independence Hall. Three serials run in the issue: Little Polly Prentiss, With Washington at Valley Forge and A Daughter of the Forest.

The first story is The Double Peril by George Coomer. It opens with a report that a Bengal tiger may have escaped from a sunken steamer and got ashore near the town. Other contents include The Fence Man, Midsummer Days, a Fourth of July piece and Wood-Folk Talk. The issue is a fair sample of the wholesome fare then sold to American children.
67636-the-useful-arts-employed-in-the-co:
The Useful Arts Employed in the Construction of Dwelling Houses, in its second edition, was printed in London by Parker of the West Strand in 1851. The book takes up the trades that build a house, and its preface starts far back. The dwellings of mankind begin rude and simple, and grow in complexity as their builders advance in civilization.

A Hottentot's hut, the preface argues, is an inverted nest, no cleverer than the nests of many birds. The bird's wants are few and its nest is remade each year. Man, once he feels himself a responsible being, outgrows the hut. He makes tools and must shelter them, grows grain and needs a store-house, gathers the wisdom of those before him and needs a roof over it. Fire, too, must be kept and guarded, and so the house, with all its arts, becomes necessary.
71629-i-ll-dream-of-you:
Charles Myers wrote I'll Dream of You, a tale first printed in Fantastic Adventures in January 1947. Toffee was just a girl in the dreams of Marc Pillsworth, the blurb says. Then he awoke one day to find the dream a reality. The tale opens under a tree, where Toffee leans back and runs a hand through her red hair. Her green eyes trace his profile and find it, if not classic, highly satisfactory.

Kiss me, she says, and Marc begs for restraint as he stares ahead. The countryside spreads before them in a sort of informal gaiety, unaware of its own stateliness. Toffee calls herself beautiful and twice as much fun as the view. Myers gives a playful tale of a dream girl made real.
77579-the-youth-of-madame-de-longueville:
The Youth of Madame de Longueville is a biography from the French of Victor Cousin. Ricord translated it for this New York edition of 1854. Appleton published the volume in that year. Its subtitle promises new revelations of court and convent in the seventeenth century.

An introduction weighs the lady's person, wit, and character in turn. Her conduct in the Fronde, the great revolt, is explained there. The first chapter covers the years from 1619 to 1635. The heroine begins life as Mademoiselle de Bourbon, in a princely family. Her mother was a Montmorency, her brother the Duke d'Enghien. The Carmelite convent of Paris gave her part of her schooling. At fifteen she appeared at a ball of the Louvre, in 1635. The second chapter follows her into the salon of the Rambouillet house.
77868-loup-garou:
Wallace West wrote a tale transcribed from Weird Tales of October 1927, where a picture caption shows a man staring as a monstrous change takes place in a wolf. Gil Couteau sits in warm courtyard sunlight, polishing his long, straight sword. The sword is good, he muses, scraping at a dark stain in the scrollwork hilt. Yet it grows thirsty from lack of use.

Couteau used it almost daily against the Saracens in Palestine. Now he leans back against the wall in sleepy comfort. It is good, he decides, to be done with slicing heads from infidels. The title names the werewolf of French lore. West sets that lore among crusader veterans home from war.
britannica-1911-anjou:
Anjou is the old name of a French territory. Its political origin lies with the Gallic Andes. Caesar's conquest organised their Roman civitas. The Andecavi gave that district its name. Frankish rule preserved it as a district. It became first a pagus, then a countship. The countship matched the diocese of Angers closely. Most of it is now Maine-et-Loire department.

Boundaries receive careful treatment in the entry. Maine bordered Anjou on the north. Touraine lay to the east. Poitiers and the Mauges bounded the south. Nantes closed the western side. Towns like Craon and Le Lude fell inside. Montreuil-Bellay and Cholet fell outside. Charles the Bald's reign opens the political narrative. The long history follows counts and their wars. Halphen's scholarship anchors this major territorial survey.
britannica-1911-bayou:
Bayou, said like “bai-yoo,” is probably a worn-down form of the French boyau, meaning gut. In the lower course of a river it names an “ox-bow” lake left behind when the stream gives up its old channel. Palmyra Lake below Vicksburg and parts of the Osage river in Missouri give clear cases.

A river swinging in wide curves eats at the bank where a bend leaves the main stream. In flood the water cuts through the neck of the bend and takes the shorter path. The old curve is then stranded, filled with dead water, while the river runs straight past it in the new channel.
britannica-1911-coustou:
Coustou is the name of a famed family of French sculptors. Nicolas Coustou (1658–1733) was the son of a wood-carver at Lyons, where he was born. At eighteen he moved to Paris to study under Coysevox, his mother's brother. Coysevox then headed the new Academy of Painting and Sculpture. At twenty-three Nicolas won the Colbert prize. That prize gave him four years of study at the French Academy at Rome.

He rose in time to rector and chancellor of the Academy. From 1700 he worked hand in hand with Coysevox at the palaces of Marly and Versailles. Speed of hand marked his work above all. Michelangelo and Algardi shaped his style most. His Seine and Marne and his Saône stand in the Tuileries gardens. A Descent from the Cross hangs behind the choir altar of Notre Dame. His younger brother Guillaume shares the family fame.
britannica-1911-margaret-of-anjou:
Margaret of Anjou is a royal life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a queen of England. She was born on the twenty-third of March 1430 and died in 1482. She was a daughter of Rene of Anjou, who claimed the crowns of Naples and Jerusalem. At fourteen she was betrothed to King Henry the Sixth.

The next year she was brought to England and wed at Titchfield Abbey in April 1445. London welcomed her with a great pageant, and she was crowned at Westminster. The duke of Suffolk had arranged the match, and he and his wife were her only friends at first. She fell under his sway and backed his policy. That, with her French birth and leanings, made her unpopular from the start.
britannica-1911-pictou: Pictou is a seaport and port of entry in Nova Scotia, noted in a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The town is the capital of Pictou county and stands ninety miles north east of Halifax. A branch of the Intercolonial railway serves it. Its count in 1901 came to 3,235 people. The entry names its chief role. Pictou is the shipping port for the coal mines nearby. Its Academy, founded in 1818, held a key place in the early schooling history of the province.
britannica-1911-sou:
Sou, the name of the bronze five centime coin of France, is explained in a money entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word is still used in France in daily reckoning. A franc is called a piece of twenty sous, and larger coins take like names. The sou comes from the Latin solidus, at first a gold coin.

Constantine first struck the solidus in gold in about the year 312, to take the place of the aureus. In the east it stayed the standard gold coin until 1453. In the west, gold coinage stopped and the solidus turned to silver. Under Charlemagne one pound of silver made twenty sols or two hundred forty deniers. That set of livre, sol, and denier served France until the Revolution. It also left its mark on the British signs for pounds, shillings, and pence.
cactus-culture-for-amateurs-being-descri:
W. Watson, aide keeper at the Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew, wrote a cactus guide for home growers, printed at London in 1889. Rich plates fill the book. Plant traits, culture, and breed work open the frame. Then genus follows genus in turn.

Epiphyllum and Phyllocactus come first. Cereus, Echinocactus, and Echinopsis fill the mid-run. Melocactus, Pilocereus, and Mamillaria come next. Leuchtenbergia, Pelecyphora, Opuntia, Pereskia, and Rhipsalis close the plant list. Heat charts, a list of cactus sellers, and a species index end the book. Scarcely six of some thousand known kinds win English favour, the first chapter owns. That slight is the gap the book fills. Pot, glass house, and warm shelf form its ground.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-chante:
Claude Chantelou, a patristic scholar, was born in 1617 at Vion in the Diocese of Le Mans and died on 28 November 1664 at Saint-Germain-des-Pres in Paris. He left the Order of Fontevrault for the Benedictines of Saint-Maur. He professed at Toulouse on 7 February 1640. In 1651 the General Chapter ordered a history of the congregation by two religious, and Chantelou, one appointee, lived at Saint-Germain-des-Pres until his death.

His Bibliotheca Patrum ascetica of 1661 to 1664 gathers extracts from the Fathers on the spiritual life. His 1662 edition of Saint Bernard's sermons adds a life of the saint by Alain of Auxerre and a life of Saint Malachy of Armagh. In 1664 he published Saint Basil's answers to his monks on monastic life. His map of Benedictine France appeared in 1726, and he helped publish D'Achery's Spicilegium.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-de-vis:
Claude de Visdelou was born at the Chateau de Bienassis in Brittany on 12 August 1656 and died at Pondicherry on 11 November 1737. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1673 and sailed for China in 1687 with Louis the Fourteenth's missionaries. He mastered Chinese language and literature. Fellow Jesuits thought he trusted modern commentators too far, since those atheist and materialist writers read their own ideas into the ancient sages.

When legate Tournon reached China in 1705 to settle the Chinese Rites, Visdelou alone among Jesuits favoured prohibiting them. Tournon named him Vicar Apostolic of Kwei-chou and Bishop of Claudiopolis, but superiors opposed the nomination, as he lacked dispensation from his vow against dignity. Secretly consecrated at Macao in February 1709, he reached Pondicherry that June and lived retired with the French Capuchins until death. His Tartar history, drawn from Chinese sources, supplemented Herbelot's Bibliotheque orientale in 1779.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-pal:
Francisco Palou, born at Palma in Majorca about 1722 and dead in 1789 or 1790, was a Franciscan friar and historian of the California missions, inseparable from Junipero Serra. He entered the Franciscans at Palma, began philosophy under Serra in 1740, volunteered with him for the American Indian missions, and joined the missionary College of San Fernando in Mexico. With Serra he worked in the Sierra Gorda missions until 1759, then in Texas country, then in Mexico City until 1767.

Sent with Serra and fourteen other friars to Lower California, he took charge of Mission San Francisco Javier in April 1768. When Serra left to found Upper California, Palou became presidente, or superior, of the lower missions. There he fought a long struggle with the hostile Governor Phelipe Barri, defeating schemes against missionaries and Indians. When the Dominicans took the peninsula missions in 1773, he followed Serra north.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-catr:
Francois Catrou, born at Paris on 28 December 1659 and dead there on 12 October 1737, was a French Jesuit historian, preacher, and journalist. Son of Mathurin Catrou, secretary to Louis XIV, he showed a graceful facility in composition at college and entered the Society at eighteen. After probation and study his preaching talent emerged. From 1690 he preached for ten years with remarkable success, and in 1701 he founded the Journal de Trevoux, serving its staff actively for twelve years.

His fame rests chiefly on historical research done alongside journalism. His general history of the Mogul empire, drawn mainly from the Venetian traveller Manuzio's memoirs, appeared in five volumes in 1715 and was translated into Italian and English. A controversial history of fanaticism in Protestant religion treated Anabaptists and Quakers. His Roman history with geographical and critical notes ran to twenty-one quarto volumes between 1725 and 1737, edited again in his last year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-augus:
French historian Jacques Auguste de Thou was born at Paris on 8 October 1553. He died there on 7 May 1617. His father Christophe was first president of the Parlement of Paris. Jacques studied at several French universities, notably Valence, where he knew Scaliger. He sought out the great minds of his age wherever he traveled. In Italy with ambassador Paul de Foix, he met Muretus, Manutius, the Pithous, and Montaigne.

In Guienne he met Henry of Navarre, the future Henry IV. As master of petitions in 1585 and councillor of state in 1588, he opposed the League. After the Duke of Guise's murder, he helped reconcile Henry III with Henry of Navarre in April 1589. He then went to Germany with Gaspard de Schomberg. They sought Protestant princes' aid against the League. The entry presents a historian-statesman of the wars of religion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kwei-chou:
Kwei-chou is a vicariate apostolic covering a mountainous Chinese province, peopled by Chinese settlers and Miao-tze tribes. A Portuguese Jesuit first carried the faith there near the end of the sixteenth century.

Paris mission priests took charge in stages: Mgr Pallu became administrator in 1658, and from 1769 Mgr Potier sent a native priest every two years to scattered Christian families. Martyrdoms mark the story, from Joseph Chang Ta-pong beheaded in 1815 to Jerome Lu Pin-mei and companions in 1858 and four Christians at Tsin-gai in 1861. Detached from Sze-ch'wan in 1846 under Father Stephen Albrand, the mission grew through the 1860 Peking treaty's promise of religious liberty.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-cous:
Nicholas Coustou, French sculptor, was born at Lyons on 9 January 1658 and died at Paris on 1 May 1733. Son of a wood-carver, he learned art first from his father. At eighteen he went to Paris and studied under his uncle, sculptor Coysevox. On Colbert's last visit to the Royal Academy, Coustou won the gold medal for sculpture, the Colbert prize, funding Rome study as pensioner from 1683 to 1686.

There he studied Michelangelo and Algardi especially, hoping to unite the one's strength with the other's grace. Returning to Paris, he showed independence by refusing the ruling sculpture school's decrees. When officials refused his design for a public monument, he went straight to the king, who ruled for him and gave him the commission. His younger brother Guillaume, also a sculptor, shared his labours, so particular works are not always easy to assign. In 1720 Nicolas became academy rector until death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-de-th:
Nicolas de Thou, bishop of Chartres and uncle of historian Jacques-Auguste de Thou, steered his city through the French Wars of Religion. Born at Paris in 1528, he became canon of Notre-Dame in 1547 and bishop in 1573, while his townspeople backed the Catholic League.

De Thou temporized, then welcomed Henry of Navarre in 1591, backed the bishops who voided Gregory XIV's ban on Henry, and stood by at Henry's abjuration. When Reims stayed in League hands, he was charged with crowning Henry IV at Chartres, acting for the archbishop of Reims.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-pithou:
Pierre Pithou was a French lawyer and scholar whose book on the liberties of the Gallican church shaped church-state relations in France for a century. He was born at Troyes in 1539 to a father who had secretly embraced Calvinism. He studied law under Cujas and was called to the Paris bar in 1560. After the wars of religion he joined the Catholic Church in 1573.

A loyal supporter of Henry IV against the Catholic League, he helped write the Satire Ménippée. In 1594 he published Les libertés de l'église gallicane, codifying in eighty-three articles the traditional freedoms of the French church from Rome. Later kings and courts treated its maxims almost as law, and he also edited classical authors and the body of canon law.
contemporary-american-literature-bibliog:
Contemporary American Literature: Bibliographies and Study Outlines, by John Matthews Manly and Edith Rickert, was published in New York by Harcourt, Brace and Company in 1922. It is a student's map of a living field. Front sections list indexes and critical periodicals, general works of reference, anthologies, and collections of plays, short stories, and essays.

The body of the book is an alphabetical index of authors, running from page 1 to 167, with biographical matter, bibliographies, and studies and reviews for each name. Indexes of authors according to form, birthplace, and subject matter or local color close the volume. Entries give a writer's books with dates, then the criticism: portraits and pages in the Bookman, the Book Buyer, and the Book Review Digest, year by year.
doe-osti-17084203-from-geometry-to-inter:
Alexander Cerjan, Catalin Spataru, and Wei Pan of Sandia develop a real space route to material topology in report SAND2026-26665R, printed September 2026. Topological materials host protected states at their edges, prized for sturdy transport in electronics and quantum devices. Standard theory finds them through band structure math in momentum space, which fails for messy or nonlinear systems.

Chapters instead probe topology with numerical K-theory, local Chern markers that read topology spot by spot, and multivariable pseudospectrum tools. Test cases include nonlinear topological materials and artificial quantum materials built in the lab. A closing part treats dynamic and driven systems. The aim is spotting interface states straight from geometry, with no band structure required.
doe-osti-3001675-nitronet-smart-system-t:
Mark Zondlo of Princeton reports for ARPA-E award DE-AR0001385, submitted 16 July 2025 after a project running May 2021 to August 2024, on farming's exhaust. Cropland is the largest human source of nitrous oxide, the third most important greenhouse gas. It escapes in hot spots and hot moments: bursts tied to fertiliser, rain, soil and microbes that defy easy measurement. Without better numbers, the climate ledger of biofuel crops stays guesswork.

NitroNet's answer is an optical web. Eye safe laser beams crisscross a field to sensors, and tomographic reconstruction turns readings into a map of emissions, a kind of CT scan for a farm field. Intelligent Material Solutions, Ethos Connected and EcoFluxNet built and deployed the system with the Princeton team. The report documents the instrument and field deployments. It records what the maps revealed about emission patterns, closing with the path toward greenhouse gas accounting for farms.
doe-osti-3020763-utility-managed-distrib:
PacifiCorp's final technical report for DOE award DE-EE0009782, dated February 20, 2026, closes the UDERMS iCommunity project, a Building Technologies Office effort to run spread-out energy resources as one utility-managed fleet. The idea was to connect multifamily, commercial, institutional, and industrial buildings so their heaters, chargers, and batteries could deliver grid services. Partners included Utah universities, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, and OSI. The project ran from June 2022 until it was shut down on October 9, 2025.

The team completed grid modeling for all participating sites and tested its resource manager against a new energy management system in a sandbox test bed. Crews fitted advanced meters and connected about 170 vehicle charging stations at pilot sites. Demand response options for water heaters and HVAC retrofits were weighed. The report records the design, cybersecurity, and business model work finished before the project ended.
doe-osti-3029162-partnership-center-for-:
Scott Parker of the University of Colorado Boulder filed this final report on April 14, 2026, for cooperative agreement DE-SC0018271. It is the university's part of the Partnership Center for High-fidelity Boundary Plasma Simulation, led by C S Chang at Princeton. The edge of a tokamak plasma decides how heat escapes, and two gyrokinetic codes, XGC and GEM, attack it from different sides. Colorado's work compared and then coupled them.

Global GEM simulations of two DIII-D L-mode cases found the core dominated by ion temperature gradient turbulence and the edge by trapped electron modes. Significant turbulence spreads inward from the edge, a candidate explanation for the transport shortfall against experiment. The GEM and XGC codes were coupled with the Dominski spatial scheme and checked against an XGC reference case with excellent agreement. The cases cover near-circular geometry and a DIII-D equilibrium with divertor.
doe-osti-3365411-mitigation-for-the-demo:
Desert Research Institute cultural resources report LR120424-1-MIT, by Megan Stueve and submitted September 2025, documents preservation mitigation before demolition of a building foundation in Area 25 of the Nevada National Security Site. Building 25-3113/3113A was itself demolished in 2005; only its concrete foundations remain, posted with signs warning of underground radioactive material. The building went up in 1958, with the 3113A addition in 1960.

Standard mitigation produced an updated resource assessment form with photographs, drawings, and an eligibility check, plus this letter report. The foundations vary in height and decay. Twenty-two accessory resources tie to the property, including a trolley line whose poles, pulleys, and motor platform the form describes in detail. Recording stands in when a Cold War structure cannot stay.
doe-osti-3383527-integration-of-goes-dat:
National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-5D00-100342, dated July 2026, integrates GOES satellite data into solar resource assessment for the contiguous United States. Five authors are printed: Yu Xie, Manajit Sengupta, Brandon Benton, Aron Habte, and Jaemo Yang. GOES, the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites, watch the same hemisphere continuously, which makes them the backbone of the National Solar Radiation Database.

The report walks through how GOES data feeds that database, then takes up blending, the step that merges satellite estimates with other data. The current blending algorithm is described first. A new algorithm follows, built on an analysis of how the bias in global horizontal irradiance behaves, and the new model is then evaluated against the old. Solar developers size real projects on this data, so bias corrections of this kind carry money with them.
doe-osti-3399533-improving-marine-energy:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory summary PNNL-SA-224924, dated July 2026 and authored by Curtis J. Larimer, is the abstract record for CRADA 679, Improving Marine Energy Production Through Commercialization of a Low-Cost, Drag-Reducing Slippery Coating. The partner names printed with it are The Mill, Prometheus Innovations, River Connectivity Systems, Lorama Group, and Dry Surface Technologies.

Marine energy devices, tidal and wave machines, lose output to two surface problems: water drag, and fouling growth that roughens blades and hulls. A slippery coating that cuts drag addresses both at once, and a low-cost one could be applied across a fleet rather than nursed as a laboratory finish. The cooperative project carried such a coating toward commercial sale. The hosted text is the project's abstract sheet, so the record stands at that summary level.
gourlay-petition-of-robert-f-gourlay-to-:
Robert F. Gourlay asks, in this 1846 petition, to be heard at the bar of the House or before a committee. The heart of the piece is a committee report from Kingston, dated September 11, 1841, signed by W. Dunlop as chairman. The report urges the legislature to declare Gourlay's sentence of banishment null and void, and to see him compensated for losses from what it calls an unwarrantable exercise of authority.

The report also recalls that, during the late rebellion, Gourlay gave Sir Francis Bond Head, then lieutenant governor of Upper Canada, key intelligence on the brigands gathering to attack the province. The petition traces how the report was debated, sustained, and then left hanging. It is a short, pointed document in a long fight: a banished reformer asking the law to own its wrong.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BurressLou_Burr:
Three weeks after the assassination, tips were still reaching the FBI from every direction. This memorandum, dated December 13, 1963, records one from Lou Burress of Dallas, who reported overhearing something about Lee Harvey Oswald and Jack Ruby.

Burress reported that Oswald had applied for work at a New Orleans hardware company and had listed Jack Ruby, the nightclub owner who later shot him, as a reference. Any paper linking Oswald and Ruby before November 24 mattered enormously, so the Bureau wrote the tip down and filed it for checking. The single memo survives as one of thousands of leads the investigation absorbed.
govdocs-archive_org-schauberger-viktor-o:
Viktor Schauberger, an Austrian forester and naturalist, argued that modern technology breaks the laws of nature and wastes human effort. Our Pointless Work presses that charge in full, with water and the forest at its center.

Schauberger watched streams and woods for decades and concluded that machines should copy nature's spirals and cycles, not fight them. He saw dammed rivers, heated water, and cleared forests as proof of a deeper error in how engineers think. The book became a classic of ecological thought, read by people who want a science that works with living systems instead of against them.
in-the-catskills-selections-from-the-wri:
John Burroughs wrote of the Catskill Mountains in essays gathered here in Boston in 1910. Clifton Johnson supplied photographs, including Slide Mountain, the highest of the Catskills. Chapters open with snow-walkers and a white day with a red fox. Farm life and hemlock woods follow.

Birds' nests get a full chapter, noting how color and nest shape relate. Speckled trout and a bed of boughs close the set. Burroughs marvels at winter as much as summer, finding the core of the world still there. The book is a calm walk with a lifelong watcher.
insights-and-heresies-pertaining-to-the-:
Ammyeetis, who signed as Persian, set out Insights and Heresies Pertaining to the Evolution of the Soul in a second edition of 1916. The book was first copyrighted in Boston in 1913. Its dedication honors minds that can say my soul is my own. Emerson lending his Plato to a farmer opens the preface with a smile.

Short pieces treat evolution, world making, death as a benefactor, and the origin of evil. Reembodiment, or rebirth in the flesh, is a central teaching. The soul, Ammyeetis argues, is carried from life to life by law. Understanding that law, the book holds, answers charges of injustice.
miss-lou:
E. P. Roe dedicated this novel, volume nine of his works, to his youngest daughter, little Miss Lou. The story opens with a girl's protest. Chapters introduce Mad Whately, his idea of courtship, and Aun' Jinkey, whose policy and warnings steer the Southern household. A storm begins, dangers thicken, and shame paralyzes the heroine.

Later chapters carry titles like Miss Lou Emancipated and A Smile on War's Grim Face. The war reaches into the courtship and tests every loyalty. Roe, a hugely popular novelist of his day, mixes romance with moral crisis. The closing chapter named in the contents promises the joy of freedom.
nasa-tm-19690004234-a-set-of-360-fortran:
Lois T. Dellner of Lewis Research Center documents a set of Fortran subroutines for printed plots in this report. The routines target IBM 360 Fortran IV at level G or H. They let programmers add plots to normal printed output without special plotting hardware.

The subroutines are simplified so beginners face few choices. Experienced programmers can still set plotting characters, scales, grid appearance, and other options. Output records run up to 132 characters for on-line or off-line printing. A user manual covers the main plotting routine and a multiple-plot routine. Scaling, sorting, and error message sections complete the documentation. The set served engineers who needed quick graphs from batch computer runs.
nasa-tm-19700002590-results-of-an-experi:
William W. Clever II of Marshall Space Flight Center reports a turbulent boundary layer control test in this September 1969 report. The wind tunnel test used wall rougheners as the control means. Roughness trips and thickens the slow air layer hugging a surface, which can serve test purposes.

Clever presents the method as simple, efficient, and capable of predictable results. Boundary layer thickness increases on the order of one hundred percent were shown, the abstract states. Controlled thick boundary layers help simulate flight conditions in ground facilities. They also help engineers study flows where a thin tunnel boundary layer would mislead the results. The report gives the experimental basis for the roughener approach.
nasa-tm-19700025219-performance-evaluati:
Pat B. McLaughlin wrote this Manned Spacecraft Center internal note, number MSC-EP-R-67-41. It evaluates a liquid-shrouded cryogenic storage system. Cryogenic systems store very cold liquids, such as the fuels and oxygen used in space flight, and keeping them cold is the whole problem.

The test program runs the storage vessel through a set of measured trials. Early tests gauge how fast shroud nitrogen boils away, first without vapor cooling and then with it. Later tests check oxygen held on nonvented standby, a minimum flowrate run with the shroud empty, and hydrogen in the shroud. Each trial's results are then discussed in turn.
pierre-grassou:
Honore de Balzac's short novel Pierre Grassou, translated by Katharine Prescott Wormeley, takes its name from a painter and opens with a long look at the Paris art world. Balzac dedicated it to a lieutenant-colonel of artillery, Periollas, as a mark of affectionate esteem.

The opening argues that since the revolution of 1830 the true Salon no longer exists. Where juries once chose two hundred paintings and crowned a masterpiece, the Louvre galleries now hold a crowded bazaar of historical pictures, landscapes, flowers, and water-colors. Balzac says the public, forced to choose for itself, soon tires. Against that scene of swollen, unjudged art, the story of Grassou and his career unfolds.
podcast-dannyjones-elXMAFc7joU:
Machine learning researcher Nathan Crock maps the future of AI in episode 11 of the KONCRETE podcast with Danny Jones. The early episode catches the field before the chatbot boom made AI a household topic. Crock speaks as a working scientist, not a salesman.

Crock explains where learning algorithms were heading and what problems blocked the road. He and Jones talk about jobs, creativity, and how smart machines might get. The chat mixes real code-level detail with crystal-ball questions about the coming decade. Tech-curious listeners get a grounded look at the AI road ahead, from before the flood.
podcast-joerogan-n1dB2iSpeOU:
Comic and podcaster Duncan Trussell returns to the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1666. Trussell, host of his own family-hour style show, is famous for long, funny talks that slide from jokes into deep questions. With Rogan, an old friend, the chat runs free and unplanned.

The two riff on love, death, faith, and the strange shape of the universe. Trussell mixes stand-up bits with real feeling about loss and wonder. Rogan plays the straight man, grounding the flights of fancy with plain questions. Fans of either man get the warm, weird hangout both shows are known for.
podcast-tuckercarlson-5V6jljDrjOU:
Singer Aaron Lewis tells Tucker Carlson that country music filled his whole childhood. He grew up in northern New England, in deep woods country. His grandparents' home in Vermont was a safe place in hard years.

Lewis fronted the rock band Staind before turning to country songs. The title charges that radio blacklisted him for his views. He also claims labels push weak music on purpose to shape culture. Carlson draws out tales of fame and fallout. The episode mixes memoir with a grievance the music business rarely airs. His voice stays raw and unpolished throughout.
podcast-tuckercarlson-SVcSqvBKAOU:
Tucker Carlson asks why House Speaker Mike Johnson keeps doing the left's bidding. Johnson rose as a quiet conservative from Louisiana. His deals with rivals soon angered his own base.

Carlson charges that the speaker funds and backs rival priorities. He calls the pattern a betrayal of voters who won the House. The episode asks if one party truly rules Washington. No guest shares the hour; the host builds the case alone. It is a sharp lament from the right, aimed at a leader its own side chose. The charge comes from inside his own camp.
romantic-ballads-translated-from-the-dan:
George Borrow translated these romantic ballads from the Danish, in an edition printed by Jarrold and Sons of Norwich in 1913. A verse from Bowring heads the book, of roaming from rock to rock along the dashing sea. Lines from Allan Cunningham to Borrow stand before the poems.

The Death-raven, from the Danish of Oehlenschläger, leads the contents, and Fridleif and Helga from the same poet follows. Sir Middel and Aager and Eliza come from the Old Danish. Elvir-shades, The Heddybee-spectre, Sir John, and May Asda complete the list shown. Miscellaneous pieces join the ballads in the volume, as its title promises.
some-one-like-you:
James W. Foley sings the praise of a true friend in Some One Like You, under a 1916 copyright held by P. F. Volland and Co. The title poem runs in short rhymed stanzas, each built on the same refrain. Some one like you, Foley writes, makes the heart seem lighter, the day's work worth while, and the sun shine brighter, and turns a sigh half into a smile.

Later stanzas fill out the friend's shape. This is a person who stands fast near, knows the speaker and likes him for just what he is, and cheers without sham or show. The bond does not bind freedom, stays loyal in joy and grief, and grows dearer each day. Through a life of briars and roses, cloud and sun, that one thread, Foley holds, runs through all the weaving.
the-hispanic-nations-of-the-new-world-a-: William R. Shepherd wrote The Hispanic Nations of the New World. The subtitle calls it a chronicle of our southern neighbors. Yale University Press published it in New Haven in 1919. The contents list twelve chapters. Early titles include The Heritage from Spain and Portugal. Later titles include Independence or Death and The Age of the Dictators. The list ends with Pan-Americanism and the Great War. A bibliographical note follows. The pages present go no further than the front matter. The heading of chapter one also appears.
the-story-of-the-philippines-natural-ric: Murat Halstead presents this volume on America's new possessions. He covered the Philippine expedition as correspondent and historian. The book appeared in 1898. He inscribes it to the soldiers and sailors of the Army and Navy for their war work against Spain. Only the title pages and inscription appear here. They promise the Philippines' natural riches and industrial resources. Statistics, laws, customs, and scenery follow. Character sketches appear too. Interviews with Admiral Dewey, General Merritt, General Aguinaldo, and the Archbishop of Manila are promised. Halstead's chapters themselves do not appear.
then-i-ll-come-back-to-you: Larry Evans wrote Then I'll Come Back to You, illustrated by Will Stevens and copyrighted in 1915. A frontispiece caption quotes a boy who has never seen more than three houses in a clearing. He has never left the timber until today. Eight chapter titles follow, from I Don't Mind If I Do! to Greetings, Sir Gallahad! Here the book stops at its opening pages and contents, so Evans's chapters themselves are not shown.
vailima-letters-being-correspondence-add: Robert Louis Stevenson's Vailima Letters gather the letters he sent to Sidney Colvin from his Samoan home between November 1890 and October 1894. Methuen of London first issued the book in November 1895, and the copy here is the seventh edition, dated December 1908. Pages present here give the title page and the start of the contents, which list an editorial note and the first letters by date. The letters themselves are not shown, but the dates frame Stevenson's last years in the South Seas.
